nameStory: Mexican Ruellia gets its name from its native homeland of Mexico and nearby regions. It's also called Mexican petunia because its purple flowers look remarkably similar to the familiar garden petunias, though they're actually from completely different plant families. The "bluebell" part of another common name refers to its bell-shaped blooms, though again, it's not related to true bluebells.
description: Mexican Ruellia is a tropical flowering plant that's rarely seen in New England's climate. It produces showy purple, trumpet-shaped flowers that bloom for just one day before dropping off. The plant has lance-shaped leaves and grows in clumps, reaching about 1-3 feet tall. In warmer climates it's considered highly invasive, but here in New England it would struggle to survive our winters.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright purple, trumpet-shaped flowers about 2 inches across with five rounded petals that feel papery to the touch. Each bloom lasts just one day, opening in the morning and dropping by evening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem, with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel. They're typically 3-6 inches long and dark green.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps or patches through underground stems, growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple upright stems that feel somewhat succulent and break easily.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, club-shaped seed capsules that split open explosively when ripe, making a faint popping sound and shooting tiny seeds several feet away.

habitat: In New England, Mexican Ruellia would only be found as a rare garden escape or greenhouse plant, as it cannot tolerate our freezing winters. If spotted, it would likely be in protected areas near buildings, in greenhouses, or as a short-lived summer annual in disturbed, moist soils.

seasonality.spring: Not hardy in New England springs - any plants would need to be replanted annually or kept indoors until after the last frost.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season if grown as an annual, producing daily purple flowers from mid-summer through early fall in warm, protected locations.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue until first frost, when the entire plant dies back. Seed capsules may be present and actively dispersing seeds.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - completely absent from the landscape except possibly in heated greenhouses.

funFact: Mexican Ruellia flowers are so short-lived that they're sometimes called "one-day flowers" - each bloom opens in the morning and drops its petals by evening, but the plant keeps producing new flowers daily throughout the growing season!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with garden petunias, but Mexican Ruellia has opposite leaves (petunias have alternate leaves) and the flowers last only one day. Wild bergamot might also look similar, but it has square stems and a minty smell when crushed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Mexican petunia," this plant is not related to true petunias at all - it's in the acanthus family while petunias are in the nightshade family. In southern states, it's considered one of the most problematic invasive plants, but New England's cold climate provides natural protection against invasion.
compareHints: Mexican Ruellia differs from its relative Hairy Ruellia by being much taller (1-3 feet vs. under 1 foot), having smooth rather than fuzzy stems and leaves, and producing more showy purple flowers instead of small pale ones. Hairy Ruellia is also native to North America and more cold-hardy, while Mexican Ruellia is tropical and cannot survive freezing temperatures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hairy ruellia differs from its relative Mexican ruellia by being much shorter and having the characteristic soft white hairs covering the plant.
